en.title: Ordering a drink
en.summary: How to order drinks at a cafe or bar and how to make small changes to an order.

paragraphs: In a cafe the waiter asks what you would like. In this lesson you will practise ordering drinks, giving quantities and answering the usual follow-up questions.
Two friends enter a cafe in Cardiff on a cold afternoon.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: Hello. What can I get you?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: A cup of tea with milk, please.

lines.speaker: Joe
lines.text: And I will have a large coffee.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: Would you like it black or white?

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: Would you like anything to eat with that?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Could I see the menu, please? I would like a slice of cake.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: Of course. I will bring it in a moment.

paragraphs: **1. A container measures a drink.** The container is countable and the drink is not, so we say a cup of tea, two cups of tea. See Introduction to Grammar: Substantives (nouns).

blocks.html:
ContainerExample
a cup ofa cup of coffee
a glass ofa glass of orange juice
a bottle ofa bottle of water
a pint ofa pint of beer

paragraphs: **2. Ordering uses I'll have, I'd like and Could I have.** All three are polite; I'll have is the most casual. See Introduction to Grammar: Future and other tenses.

blocks.html:
PhraseExample
I'll have...I'll have a large coffee.
I'd like...I'd like a cup of tea.
Could I have...?Could I have the menu?
What can I get you?the waiter's question

items: White coffee has milk; black coffee has none.
Still water has no bubbles; sparkling water has.
Takeaway means to take away; Americans say to go.
In a British pub you order and pay at the bar.

paragraphs: Tea in Britain usually comes with a little milk, and you add sugar yourself. Coffee is more common in the United States, where the waiter will often refill your cup without being asked.
